analysis.one_liner: Bans the largest online platforms from favoring their own products over rivals on their platforms.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in June 2023 with eight bipartisan cosponsors and never received a vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for very large online platforms — those with tens of millions of American users whose owners are worth over $550 billion — to put their own products ahead of businesses that rely on the platform, use sellers' own data to compete against them, or block users from deleting preloaded apps and changing defaults. Platforms that broke the rules could face fines of up to 10% of their U.S. revenue, and repeat offenders' executives could have to give up a year of compensation. It never got a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who use dominant platforms — they would get more choice, the ability to uninstall preinstalled apps, and fairer search and app-store results — and the millions of small businesses that sell through Amazon, app stores, and search ads, who would compete against the platform owner on more equal terms.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Shoppers and small sellers on big platforms

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars a covered platform from favoring its own products over a business user's in a way that materially harms competition, and from treating its own products more favorably in search and ranking.
It bars platforms from using nonpublic data generated by business users to build competing products, and from restricting users from uninstalling preinstalled apps or changing default settings.

Enforcement rests with the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general, with civil penalties up to 10% of a violator's U.S. revenue and possible forfeiture of executive compensation for repeat offenders.

analysis.who_pays: The largest platform operators — Amazon, Apple, Google, Meta — which would face compliance costs, limits on practices like self-preferencing and bundling, and fines up to 10% of U.S. revenue; some added costs could be passed on to sellers or advertisers.

drawbacks.text: The bill's affirmative defenses — for safety, privacy, security, and 'core functionality' — are broad, and critics argued they could let platforms defend much of the very conduct the bill targets, leading to years of litigation.

Opponents warned that requiring platforms to share data and interoperate with rivals could weaken encryption, privacy, and security, and that rules like these (as in Europe's Digital Markets Act) can push companies toward workarounds rather than real change.
Compliance costs for the covered platforms would be large, and some could be passed through to the small businesses and advertisers the bill aims to help.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers and small businesses the upside is real: fairer search, no forced default apps, and no competing against the platform's own use of their data. The costs fall almost entirely on a handful of trillion-dollar companies, though some may reach sellers through fees. The biggest uncertainty is enforcement — the broad defenses and a designation process requiring FTC-DOJ agreement could dilute the bill in practice.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee in June 2023, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on June 15, 2023 with eight cosponsors — five Democrats and three Republicans, including Sen. Chuck Grassley — and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
The full action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

The bill defines covered platforms as those with 50 million or more U.S. monthly users whose owner has over $550 billion in U.S. sales or market value, or a billion or more worldwide users — a threshold aimed at a handful of very large companies.

A nearly identical version of this bill cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee 20-2 with strong bipartisan support in February 2022, but was never brought to the Senate floor, making the reintroduction's quiet death in committee a second failure for the same idea.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The dominant platform companies are better off because the bill died: their practices of favoring their own products, using sellers' data, and setting defaults remain unrestricted, while consumers and small sellers gained nothing. Senate leadership that declined to schedule the bill also avoided a vote that had drawn heavy industry opposition.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Dominant platforms, which kept current practices

for.name: Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the American Innovation and Choice Online Act in the Senate on June 15, 2023.

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start.

for.name: Six additional Senate cosponsors
for.role: Durbin (D), Graham (R), Blumenthal (D), Hawley (R), Hirono (D), Warner (D), Booker (D)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, producing an 8-member bipartisan coalition.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill — or its identical predecessor, which had cleared committee 20-2 — to the Senate floor for a vote.

against.name: Amazon, Apple, Google, and Meta
against.what_they_did: Lobbied heavily against the bill and its predecessor, funding campaigns and warnings that it would break popular features and weaken privacy and security.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred on June 15, 2023.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: of eight cosponsors, five were Democrats and three were Republicans, and the predecessor bill passed the Judiciary Committee 20-2 with members of both parties in favor; opposition came from within leadership scheduling and industry lobbying, not from a party bloc.

industries.industry: Dominant online platforms (Amazon, Apple, Google, Meta)
industries.note: The bill would directly regulate how these companies run their platforms: no self-preferencing, no using sellers' data against them, no forcing default apps, with fines up to 10% of U.S. revenue and possible executive compensation forfeiture. Because the bill died, these companies keep practices that many users and sellers say cost them money and choice.

industries.industry: Small businesses, app developers, and third-party sellers on big platforms
industries.note: These businesses would have gained the right to compete on the platform without the owner stacking the deck against them, and to port their own data to other systems. Their interest matches consumers' interest in fair search and more choices.
